Math Telepathy

DivisibilityArithmeticLogic
Game: Think of a number, shuffle its digits, subtract, and keep one digit of the answer in mind. The computer will name it.
How to play: Follow the steps on the screen. Then press the digit buttons once for every digit of your answer except the one you kept, and press Guess.

    Look for the math

    No mind reading: the computer uses the fact that a number and any shuffle of its digits leave the same remainder when divided by 9, so their difference is a multiple of 9.

    Any power of 10 is 1 mod 9

    Since 10 = 9 + 1, every power of 10 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9. A digit d standing for d · 10k in the first number and for d · 10m after shuffling contributes d(10k − 10m) to the difference, and that is a multiple of 9. So the whole difference is a multiple of 9. The test checked this for all 6,581,934 pairs of a number up to 99,999 and a different shuffle of its digits.

    A multiple of 9 has digits adding to a multiple of 9

    This is the casting out nines rule. Given every digit but one, the computer adds them and takes the remainder mod 9; the missing digit is what is needed to reach the next multiple of 9, which is 9 − (sum mod 9). When the circled digit is 9 the other digits already add to a multiple of 9, and the computer says 9 and never 0, which is right because the circled digit is not zero. All 25,607,935 circled digits of all those differences were named correctly.

    Why the warning about mistakes

    The trick lives on the difference being a multiple of 9. If the subtraction is wrong by 1, the digits add up to 1 more than a multiple of 9, and then the computer's answer cannot be the circled digit: the test found it was never right in over 29,000 tries. Check your subtraction, or use a calculator.

    Try a number with a repeated digit, such as 4,400. Does a shuffle like 0,044 still work? What is the largest circled digit you can make?
